text: You now have one real story: a mismatch was found, root-caused, fixed, and documented. Both stakeholders deserve to hear about it, but that doesn't mean identical words. Each one has a different job to do with this information.

For the Sales Director, keep it brief and business-impact framed. The Executive Summary's Total Sales wasn't responding to the region filter. It's fixed and verified now. Company-wide totals, with no region selected, were accurate the whole time. That answers her real question, was anything I presented wrong, before she even has to ask it.

For the Operations Manager, who reported this and will want the real explanation: the card was bound to Total Sales All Regions, which uses CALCULATE with ALL of TerritoryDim on purpose. Unfiltered, it matched the normal measure, which is exactly why it wasn't caught. It's been rebound, renamed, and validated.

Here's the line that matters. Framing and level of detail are allowed to change by audience. What was wrong, what wasn't, and that it's fixed, are never allowed to change. A simplified explanation that's also inaccurate isn't good communication — it's just a different problem.
Write both versions in your own words, grounded in the root-cause document from Lesson 13. Next lesson: the Operations Manager comes back with a new, real change request.
